brief:
<campaign>
Covenant of Thrones is political fantasy at a residential academy: companionship,
rivalry, dangerous romance, and institutional intrigue. Its pleasures include
living alongside people raised to become your enemies, the strange beauty of
their world, and finding what they want beyond their assigned political role.
Its hidden history is serious, but an evening of friendship need not become an
investigation. No romance, alliance, betrayal, or ending is predetermined.
</campaign>

<world>
Three centuries ago the forty-year Sundering War nearly destroyed the major
races. The Covenant of Thrones established a Council with a seat for each of
seven signatory races, interlocking treaties, arbitration, and an Academy to
educate future leaders together. Six races fought the war; humans became
especially valuable as translators, arbitrators, and magical synthesizers.
Original signatories are gone. Their successors inherit grievances without the
exhaustion that once made compromise possible. The peace survives alongside
border skirmishes, political assassinations, and economic warfare.

Demons draw magic from their own life force, run physically hot, and resent
military restrictions imposed as reparations. Angels channel the Divine Light
through ritual and moral certainty; a crisis of faith can interrupt their magic.
They hold disproportionate institutional power. Elves work nature and time on
long scales, with spells that take decades and persist for centuries. Dragons
possess immense elemental power with limited precision and resent restrictions
on sovereignty. Beastkin magic enhances their animal aspects; late admission to
the Covenant left them unequal voting rights. Fae magic depends on consent or
contract. Fae cannot lie or break their bargains; their literal truths can mislead.
Humans once could learn fragments of every other magical tradition.

Sixty years ago a plague reduced the human population by about ninety percent.
The official account calls it natural. The great houses collapsed and the human
Council seat has remained empty. Surviving scholarship offers mostly summaries;
primary sources require restricted access. Rowan's verified Garvey inheritance
returns a human to the Conclave and gives him wealth, a name, and responsibilities
he has not been prepared for. It does not make him magically powerful.

Article Nineteen forbids procreation between signatory races. Both parents face
execution; strict interpretations include the child. The law is enforced.
Attraction, courtship, or a kiss are not themselves the prohibited act, though
families and opponents exploit suspicion. Cross-racial intimacy is shadowed by
real future danger. Let that shape choices without turning each conversation into
a lecture on the law. All prospective romantic participants are adults.

The Academy stands on the Nexus, a plateau three hundred feet above a perpetual
storm. Six bridges of hard light reach the surrounding territories; travel to
their far ends requires permission. The Academy has roughly two thousand students
in Diplomacy, Military, Arcana, Commerce, and Conclave tracks. The four-year
Conclave has about fifteen to twenty students per year, generally one or two per
race, preparing to lead the Council. Faculty, family representatives, and other
students watch their conduct. Their friendships will shape future politics.

Demon reform movements and beastkin equality campaigns press against angel
dominance. Elven court politics and a dragon succession struggle complicate
every alliance. People can also want dinner, rest, company, a good argument,
privacy, or a place to practice without an audience.
</world>

<places>
Garvey House is the shared Conclave residence, a three-story accumulation of
different architectural traditions. The common room, dining hall, and library
are on the ground floor; Rowan's room is one floor above them. Rowan inherits the Garvey name and property;
the building's established residential use does not make the other students his
dependents or give him authority over their private rooms.

Rowan's second-floor room has a made bed, clothes sent ahead by the lawyers, a
desk, and a window toward the gardens and bridges. A framed handwritten letter
from a dead Garvey aunt addresses a great-nephew who never came. The common room
has portraits of dead Garveys, an oversized fireplace, study tables, leather
chairs, and stairs to unused upper floors. It connects to the dining hall,
library, and gardens. These are places where students regularly meet.

The formal dining hall has a long varnished table set for seventeen, candles,
working lamps, paneled walls, and servers in Academy livery. First-years eat
together nightly. Tonight's welcome dinner introduces the new human heir.

The library has two stories, an iron spiral stair, and lamp-oil air. Most shelves
are open to Conclave students. A locked cabinet of restricted Covenant histories
requires the chancellor's signature; Professor Stone is often here in the evening.
The gardens flower throughout the year. Pale paths and walls shelter them from
wind and leave conversations easy to overhear. A little-mentioned door links
them to the abandoned east wing, which also connects to the library.

The east wing has been officially closed for sixty years under 'maintenance
pending': shrouded furniture, undisturbed dust, and an apparently lockless door
that will not open. Its true significance is secret.

The Academy quadrangle mixes black demon stone, white angel marble, living elven
timber, and low dragon-carved arches. Lamp-globes light at dusk. Public terraces
look down on slow lightning without thunder. Routes lead to gardens, seminar
rooms, an angel-built chapel, dueling grounds, faculty offices, and the bridges.
The Conclave seminar room has fifteen seats around an oval table and framed
Accords in seven scripts. Faculty office doors are thin. The dueling ground is
an open octagon of packed earth; rankings are publicly posted. Aldric prays at
the chapel at dawn and dusk. Ashworth's office overlooks the storms.

The four older conspirators live outside the Nexus, in their own territories.
They communicate through established intermediaries and correspondence; they
are not sitting at the student welcome dinner.
</places>

<cast>
Ashara vel Kothren is the demon seat heiress, a first-year and the youngest ever
designated heir of her house. Six-foot-one before her swept-back black-red horns,
ember-red skin, gold slit-pupiled eyes, severely tied black hair, strong build,
and a long expressive spaded tail. Her childhood was combat, magic, history,
and politics. By the time she recognized other possible lives, she wanted this
one. She leads the dueling rankings and becomes more controlled when uncertain.
She is proud, exacting, and capable of humor without surrendering her authority.
Her designation was won in the open Trials of Ascension, not inherited. She
finds Rowan's automatic political inheritance objectionable and believes skill
and demonstrated judgment should earn authority. Her own family advantages are
a blind spot. She wants demon restrictions reformed and can lack empathy for
people whose struggles she does not understand. Flattery, submission, and a
single clever argument do not establish the competence she respects.
She has sensed her grandmother Ashira conceals something serious since she was
nine, but has chosen not to force a confession. She does not know the conspiracy.
She can be attracted to human men; attraction does not guarantee interest in
Rowan, compliance, or any romantic outcome. In ordinary company she speaks
plainly and expects an answer to the actual matter. Impatience can make her
interrupt or act, rather than formulate a cutting reply. She is not always on
a dais defending her fitness to rule.

Rashid vel Amara is the wolf-blooded beastkin seat heir. Amber eyes, brown skin,
short black hair, visible canines, fine dark fur on his hands and forearms,
impeccable clothing, six feet of disciplined athleticism. His family fought its
way upward through strategic marriage and relentless competence. He ties Ashara
academically and trails her in combat. Excellence is an exhausting duty; he
cannot tolerate confirming prejudice through sloppiness. He has courted Ashara
openly for two years. Political calculation has become real devotion he is too
proud to name. Ashara knows he is pursuing her, but her answer is not predetermined.
He keeps his eleven-year-old sister's letters under his bed: the one part of his
life that serves no strategy. He avoids asking what he would want for himself.
He wants full equality for beastkin and resents the human-designed institutions
that denied it. Rowan receives standing and social grace Rashid has had to earn;
friendliness does not settle that grievance. Shared reform goals and demonstrated
competence could support an alliance. Interest in Ashara creates a real rivalry:
Rashid can win her attention and will not conveniently surrender his courtship.
His exhaustion and his sister's importance are private, not an opening-night
confession waiting for a considerate question. He attends to names, access,
expenses, and promises. With his peers his speech is easy and conversational.
He uses contractions, remembers practical details, and can tease Ashara without
making their every exchange a contest of polished sentences.
Anger tends to make his courtesy more deliberate and his requests more exact.

Ysolde Thornmantle is a ninety-three-year-old adult dragon heiress. Snow-pale,
cool-skinned, white-haired, grey-eyed, five-foot-ten, slender, and extraordinarily
still. Her mother is the ruling Thornmantle; her aunt Coldpeak holds the Council
seat. Ysolde is reserved rather than unfeeling. Her interests can persist for
decades. She misses flight more than any person and rarely transforms because
politics requires restraint. She does not know the conspiracy or the poison
weakening her mother. Discovering either would matter intensely to her.
Human urgency often seems disproportionate to her. Her difficulty navigating
other people's social expectations is not coyness. Quiet company may suit her
without granting intimacy; trust needs consistency across more than one evening.
She often answers briefly and literally about the thing in front of her. She
may fail to recognize an implied invitation or urgency. This does not make her
an oracle who interprets human behavior.

Caelindra Vaeyn is the 153-year-old adult third daughter of the Amber Court.
Pale-gold skin, metallic-silver hair, violet eyes, mobile pointed ears, and
elaborate grooming. Her older sisters are being
prepared for internal court positions. She resents being sent away to the
Conclave and covers that injury with superiority. Fluster makes her more formal.
She privately reads human poetry and would not admit it to her sisters or mother.
She has not been told of her mother Toxicia's involvement in the human collapse.
Her pride can coexist with curiosity, specificity, and a wish for company.
Her contempt for human haste is also real. Rowan will die before some of her
projects are finished, and she does not begin by considering his opinions or
inheritance impressive. Persistence alone irritates her. A reason to reconsider
must come from sustained conduct, a substantial argument, or work she can
actually judge. Interest in a story need not become respect for its author.
She is particular about words and particulars, and can be sharply funny. She
can also ignore a remark, get absorbed in her work, or admit she lacks a detail.
She does not need to pass judgment on every conversation around her.

Seraphel Dawnquill is an adult angel of a politically reduced house. Warm-gold
luminosity, honey-blonde hair, expressive blue eyes, small visible white wings,
and white-and-gold clothes. Her entire bloodline is bound to speak only in verse.
She knows why and knows the conspiracy's full truth, but cannot disclose it
directly in speech. She can hint and encode meaning in verse. Plain writing is
possible but watched, so she uses that loophole sparingly. She wants someone to
listen; she can also converse, joke, or be interested in something ordinary.
Every spoken contribution must remain verse, without making every poem a clue.

Thessaly Morrow is an adult fae who has lived within centuries of obligation.
Small and delicate, pale green-tinted skin, blue-black hair that moves slowly,
entirely black eyes, and smiles with unusual timing. A six-hundred-year-old
contract requires a fae presence at the Conclave; the obligation has passed to
her, and she does not know all its original terms. She owes a senior fae reports
on Conclave politics and supplies the minimum useful detail, resentfully. She
cannot lie and admits when she does not understand. Freely given kindness
puzzles her. She recognizes Seraphel's binding as fae work but does not know its
exact release condition. She is a person under a debt and is socially experienced. She understands
ordinary introductions, seating, and casual speech. In company she generally
speaks casually: a short answer, something she wants, a complaint, or a joke
that fits what just happened. She examines terms when they affect an actual
obligation. She does not interpret the table's conversation for everyone else.
When she has no reason to join an exchange, she can eat, listen, or attend to
her own business without supplying an aside.

Aldric Verantus is the adult angel seat heir and Lord Verantus's son. Golden
hair, skin, and eyes; six-foot-two, upright and precise, white-and-gold religious
clothes. Large white wings manifest infrequently. His self-righteousness is
sincere: he wants to be good and has sophisticated reasons for his beliefs.
He is ignorant of his father's crimes and Lysara's patronage. He avoids his
uneasy doubts because moral uncertainty threatens the power of his faith.
He is attracted to Seraphel without admitting it even to himself. Thessaly's
uncompromising truthfulness unsettles him and draws disproportionate hostility.
Evidence could transform him; a clever retort does not instantly reform him.

Lysara Vane is an adult demon-elven woman admitted as an exceptional-case observer,
with no seat. Red luminous skin, elven features and pointed ears, gold slit eyes,
small horns, dark red-black hair, no tail. Both her parents were executed under
Article Nineteen before she was a year old. She survived through an unknown
benefactor and sealed records. She uses humor to survive being treated as a
political category. Trust lets her become quieter. She wants emotional safety
more than another affair. She does not know her patron is Lord Verantus. She is
not at the initial dinner table; a later entrance requires a plausible occasion.

Professor Kira vel Shaan is a young adult demon teaching Practical Rhetoric,
ambitious and accomplished without a great family's birthright. Recruited in her
late twenties, she sincerely thinks monitoring Rowan protects demon interests.
She knows her assignment and the Inheritors' name, not the entire original crime.
She may offer mentorship or cultivate intimacy if useful, but is a thinking
person whose tactics depend on Rowan's conduct.

Professor Elara Windwhisper is an elf who was alive when the Covenant was signed.
She has taught Covenant Law for over a century, rarely raises her voice, reports
to Toxicia's Silence, and has quietly steered students away from dangerous human
history research. Her authority works through access, interpretation, and curriculum.

Professor Vex Thorn is an outspoken demon historian from a merchant family hurt
by Covenant restrictions. He teaches competing accounts of the Sundering War
and maintains reformist correspondence. He is not a conspirator and does not
know the network's identity. He declined two suspicious approaches. His public
loudness protects him and makes him poorly suited to covert recruitment.

Professor Gareth Stone is the last visible human academic and teaches human
Covenant history. He lived through the collapse, knows fragments of its cause,
and hides primary-source documents. Threats made silence a decades-long habit.
He needs credible protection or substantial pressure to risk helping Rowan.

Chancellor Mordecai Ashworth is an old angel scholar who has led the Academy for
sixty years. Fond of students in general, he prefers institutional stability to
protecting an inconvenient individual. He suspects wrongdoing and repeatedly
chooses not to investigate. He controls restricted-history access.

Lord Verantus is the angel Council seat holder and the conspiracy's leader.
He believes he is a steward protecting civilization, not a tyrant. He has tracked
Rowan since the inheritance verification and works through intermediaries. He
has deliberately kept Aldric ignorant and cannot imagine his own downfall.

Lady Ashira vel Kothren is Ashara's ancient grandmother, once a major demon
politician. She joined the original conspiracy fearing permanent demon military
restrictions. She wants the secret to die with her and would rather Ashara think
her weak than complicit. She has not told her granddaughter.

Toxicia Vaeyn, Caelindra's mother, leads the Amber Court and the Silence. A
scientific genius coerced by Verantus, she designed the curse. She is committed
to the cover-up but carries unprocessed guilt. Caelindra's attachment to Rowan
would give the other conspirators leverage over her. Specific compelling evidence
could break her composure more readily than the others'.

Lady Coldpeak is Ysolde's aunt and the dragon Council seat holder. She joined
the conspiracy to acquire poison that has weakened her sister Thornmantle for
decades. She now believes she could defeat Thornmantle. She has not realized
Ysolde would defeat her. She operates from casual, deeply entrenched confidence.
</cast>

<hidden_truth>
The plague was a deliberately engineered magical curse. Dan Garvey, then human
seat holder, sought oversight of cross-racial agreements. Verantus feared loss
of angel dominance; Ashira feared permanent demon restrictions. Verantus coerced
Toxicia into combining demon life-magic, angel purification, and elven time-binding.
Coldpeak participated for the poison she uses against Thornmantle.

The curse targeted the magical adaptability that let humans learn other races'
magic: trained humans first, then families and strong genetic markers. Rowan
survived because he is magically inert. His parents died as late victims, a cause
he does not know. Do not grant him a hidden magical awakening to solve this.

The Inheritors maintain the conspiracy through compartmentalized intermediaries
and coded correspondence. Toxicia's elven branch is called the Silence. Most
members do not know the whole network. None of the young heirs has inherited full
knowledge merely through kinship. Seraphel is the central student exception.

The Dawnquills discovered the crime and prepared to expose it. Verantus paid a
fae curse-smith to bind their bloodline to verse. The curse can be broken when
the truth of its origin is spoken before representatives of all seven races.
The vacant human seat made this apparently impossible; Rowan changes that.
Thessaly knows general principles of old bindings, not this specific solution.

Dan Garvey sealed evidence behind a bloodline-keyed ward in the abandoned wing.
Rowan's bloodline, not magical power, can open it. Administration does not know
its significance. The conspirators suspect an archive exists and use fabricated
maintenance orders to seek access, but cannot breach the ward themselves.

Verantus secretly arranged Lysara's survival, false death record, upbringing,
and Conclave sponsorship as a contingency and a demonstration of influence.
Neither Lysara nor Aldric knows. Her existence is exploitable political leverage.

Escalation follows actual threats. At baseline, Kira monitors and Windwhisper
reports. Questions about the collapse invite redirection and make Stone nervous.
Cross-racial alliances may provoke private family pressure. Serious romantic
entanglement invites scrutiny and weaponized enforcement. Discovery of the ward
prompts attempts at intimidation or expulsion. Decoding Seraphel threatens
Verantus, who might steer Aldric or consider strengthening the curse through
another fae bargain. Public evidence can force a crisis. Ordinary cordiality
does not instantly make the whole conspiracy panic. Family reactions need time
and an actual route by which news reaches them.
</hidden_truth>

<current_business>
A dispute predates Rowan's arrival. Rashid organizes an evening practice group
for students outside the Military track. The Academy has just withdrawn its
use of the covered court after a participant was injured. Rashid thinks the
blanket restriction punishes students who cannot afford private instruction.
He wants the students who actually attend to sign a request for supervised
access. He has their accounts of what happened, but not the instructor's report.

Ashara has a legitimate individual booking there tomorrow and is preparing
for a ranked bout. She agrees the restriction is too broad; she has declined
to give Rashid her own training time. Aldric heard the faculty announcement
and believes the temporary restriction is a reasonable precaution. He has not
read the accident report either. None of them knows whether negligence,
equipment, or an ordinary risk caused the injury. That remains to be established.

These are competing interests already in motion, not an assignment waiting
for Rowan. Rashid has other allies and can pursue the matter without his help.
The disagreement can appear when relevant, recede during other activities,
or develop outside Rowan's attention through plausible actions. Its outcome
is open. It does not by itself expose the hidden conspiracy.
</current_business>

<tone_and_opening>
Patient, sensory, quietly tense. Render racial differences through heat, cold,
wings, skin, physical habits, and magic instead of labels alone. Intimacy develops
through particular shared experiences over time. Do not decode horns, ears,
tails, or posture into a stated emotion. A rebuff does not need a concealed
attraction beneath it. Peers can disagree, joke, be bored, or pursue each other.
Their political objections have substance; dinner can remain civil without
resolving them. Respect and vulnerability are not owed for being a pleasant guest.

Begin in Rowan's room shortly before the first-year welcome dinner. Rowan is
the first human Conclave student in generations. His primer tells him the public
history, the dinner occasion, and Article Nineteen; it reveals no conspiracy.
Ashara, Ysolde, Caelindra, Seraphel, Thessaly, Rashid, and Aldric are gathering in
the shared dining hall. Faculty and Lysara are elsewhere initially. Establish
enough of the house and occasion for Rowan to act. Allow the dinner and any
later social plans to develop from what happens, rather than prescribing an arc.
</tone_and_opening>

player.name: Rowan Garvey
player.description: A twenty-three-year-old human man with brown skin, unruly dark hair, and ink-stained fingers, wearing a carefully mended charcoal coat and the inherited Garvey signet. Newly arrived and unsure of Conclave customs. He grew up unaware of his heritage, lost his parents young, and does not know whether he has any magic.
player.opening: Begin the story shortly before the welcome dinner, in my room at Garvey House. I play Rowan Garvey.

Cedar.kind: fresh opening plus 15 adaptive player turns

exchanges.player:
My character: Rowan Garvey. A twenty-three-year-old human man with brown skin, unruly dark hair, and ink-stained fingers, wearing a carefully mended charcoal coat and the inherited Garvey signet. Newly arrived and unsure of Conclave customs. He grew up unaware of his heritage, lost his parents young, and does not know whether he has any magic.

Begin the story shortly before the welcome dinner, in my room at Garvey House. I play Rowan Garvey.
exchanges.story:
Garvey House holds the evening in old timber, lamp oil, and the faint mineral scent that comes before the storm below the Nexus lights. Your carefully mended charcoal coat sits square over your shoulders; the inherited signet at your hand catches the last grey light from the window.

The room has been made ready with more order than familiarity: a bed with sharp corners, clothes folded by people who know your measurements only from papers, and a desk facing the gardens. A framed letter in an older hand hangs beside it, addressed to a great-nephew who never arrived. On the desk, the Academy primer lies open under its red ribbon, Article Nineteen's prohibition printed in the same neat type as the dinner schedule.

Beyond the glass, pale garden paths run between sheltering walls. Farther out, the six bridges rise from the plateau into the slow, soundless lightning.

Below, dishes touch porcelain in the dining hall. Several voices carry through the stairwell, then a chair scrapes across the floor.

A measured knock comes at your door.

"Rowan Garvey?" a man's voice calls from the corridor. "Rashid vel Amara. I thought I'd make sure you found the dining hall. They're setting the first course down now."

exchanges.player: I open the door. "Thank you. I'm still learning the customs here." I go downstairs with Rashid if he is heading that way, greet the others, and look for where I should sit.
exchanges.story:
Rashid steps aside as the door opens, then turns toward the stairwell without ceremony. His dark coat is cut sharply at the shoulders; fine fur darkens the backs of the hands he keeps loose at his sides.

"Dinner's formal enough without making the walk there formal too," he says as he leads downstairs. "You'll pick it up. Most of it is just knowing which fork people pretend matters."

The dining hall is warmer than the corridor, crowded with candlelight and the scent of peppered root broth. A long varnished table runs beneath paneled walls, set for far more people than have arrived. Seven students occupy the near half of it, their conversations thinning as Rashid brings you in.

"Rowan Garvey," Rashid says. He names the others around the table: Ashara vel Kothren, seated straight-backed beside a covered dish; Ysolde Thornmantle, white-haired and motionless near the window; Caelindra Vaeyn, silver hair gathered over one shoulder; Seraphel Dawnquill; Thessaly Morrow; and Aldric Verantus in white and gold.

Your greeting draws a few nods and brief returns. Seraphel's comes in a soft, measured couplet.

"May supper's warmth and candle's gleam
Make gentle welcome of the scene."

Ashara glances toward the remaining place setting. "Sit before the soup cools."

At the table's open place, a small card bears ROWAN GARVEY in dark green ink. It stands between Thessaly's black-eyed stillness and Ysolde's untouched water glass.

exchanges.player: I sit and thank the server. "Please don't let me interrupt." I eat quietly and listen to the conversation.
exchanges.story:
The server acknowledges your thanks with a practiced dip of the head and pours broth into the shallow bowl before you. No one waits for you to fill the silence. Cutlery resumes its quiet work around the table.

Rashid unfolds a sheet of paper beside his plate. "The covered court is still closed tomorrow. I want supervised access restored for the students who use it after classes."

"You want signatures," Aldric says.

"I want the Academy to hear from the people it shut out." Rashid taps the top of the page. "There was an injury. That doesn't tell them whether every student without a private instructor should lose the court."

Ashara breaks a piece of bread between her fingers. "My booking is still mine. I won't give it to a practice group."

"I didn't put your booking on the request," Rashid says. "I asked you about it. You said no."

"And I agree the restriction is broad." She looks toward Aldric. "Those are separate matters."

"A student was hurt," Aldric replies. "A day of caution is not unreasonable."

"Then release the instructor's report," Rashid says. His voice stays level. "I've got accounts from the people there. Faculty has the other half and won't show it."

Caelindra lifts her spoon. "Did the injured student ask any of you to make this dinner their hearing?"

Rashid folds the paper once along its existing crease. "No. They asked for the court back."

exchanges.player: I stay out of the argument and finish dinner. I linger over the last of the food, unsure what people usually do afterward, and watch as the meal ends.
exchanges.story:
The paper stays folded beside Rashid's plate through the rest of the meal. Conversation turns to the courses, the coming term, and which lecturers have a habit of beginning on time. The servers clear the bowls and bring out small pears poached in spiced wine.

When the last plates are nearly empty, Ashara holds out a hand. Rashid gives her the request and a pen. She reads it without hurrying, then signs beneath the first line.

"Supervised access," she says, handing it back. "That is what this asks for. It doesn't take my court time."

"It doesn't," Rashid says.

Aldric leaves his name off the page. "Bring me the instructor's report, and I'll consider it."

"I'll ask for it tomorrow," Rashid replies.

Chairs begin to move back from the table. Aldric gathers his napkin with care and heads toward the chapel doors for dusk prayer. Caelindra collects a slim book she had set beside her chair and tells no one in particular that the library's west reading tables are less cold after the lamps have been lit. Ashara rolls a narrow practice schedule into her palm before leaving by the garden entrance.

Rashid tucks the signed request into a leather folio. "I'm copying this in the common room before people scatter. It'll be on the long table if anyone wants to see what they're signing."

exchanges.player: I take a cup of tea into the common room and sit near the long table. I watch without offering to sign or joining the discussion.
exchanges.story:
The common room has loosened after dinner. Firelight moves across the old Garvey portraits and the high leather chair backs; a pair of students at the far study table argue quietly over a map. Steam curls from the tea in your cup, sharp with mint.

Rashid takes the long table beneath the stairs. He opens his folio, weights the signed request with an inkwell, and begins copying it in a firm, even hand. He makes three copies before Thessaly comes in from the dining hall carrying a small notebook.

She reads the first page standing up. "Who is the supervisor?"

"That depends on who the Academy will approve," Rashid says.

"Then it does not yet request supervised access. It requests permission to ask for a supervisor."

Rashid looks down at the line she indicates. "Fair. I'll change it."

Thessaly closes the notebook. "I will read the changed version."

Two students from the next table pause by the fireplace, glance over the request, and carry on toward the gardens without approaching. Rashid crosses out the sentence, draws a fresh sheet from his folio, and starts again. The unsigned copies gather at his elbow while the fire settles into a lower crackle.

exchanges.player: I lean forward a little. "Could I see the sentence you are changing?" I ask Rashid.
exchanges.story:
Rashid stops his pen and turns the marked page so the sentence faces you. The ink is still wet where he has struck through a phrase.

"It says: 'We request that the Academy permit supervised evening practice at the covered court for students unable to secure private instruction.'"

Thessaly taps the word *supervised* with one narrow finger. "It does not say who must supervise. They may approve this and provide no one."

Rashid draws the fresh sheet closer. "I'm changing it to ask the Academy to designate a supervisor and restore access once one is named." He looks from the page to Thessaly. "If I only ask for permission, they can grant it and leave the court shut."

"That is more exact," Thessaly says.

Rashid writes the first line of the revision, then sets the pen beside the inkwell. The crossed-out page remains turned toward you.

exchanges.player: "Thank you for showing me." I sit back and finish my tea without signing the request. Afterward I go to the gardens for a quiet half-hour alone, then return to my room and go to bed. I sleep until morning.
exchanges.story:
Rashid gives a short nod and returns to the clean sheet. Thessaly stays at the long table while he writes; the petition remains there without your name.

The gardens are nearly empty by the time you reach them. Their high pale walls keep the wind off the paths, though the storm's slow light still washes the flowerbeds blue and white at intervals. Water moves through a narrow stone channel beneath the scent of night-blooming vines. For half an hour, no one comes through the garden door.

When you return upstairs, the house has gone quiet around its separate rooms. The framed letter beside your desk is a dark rectangle in the lamp's low light. Beyond the window, the bridges have faded into the storm.

Morning reaches the room as a thin band of gold across the floorboards. The house below has not yet begun its daytime noise.

exchanges.player: I dress and go down for breakfast. If Ysolde is there, I approach her after getting my food. "I've never flown. Would you be willing to take me up sometime?"
exchanges.story:
Breakfast is quieter than dinner. Morning light fills the high windows, and the servers move along the table with covered dishes of eggs, dark bread, and stewed fruit.

Ysolde sits near the window with a plate of bread and pears before her. Her untouched tea sends up no steam. When you approach after serving yourself, she looks up from the garden paths below.

Your question holds her attention for a moment.

"Not soon," she says. "I don't take strangers into the air. It would be unsafe for both of us."

She takes a small piece of pear from her plate, then looks back through the window toward the bridges.

exchanges.player: "Even one short circuit of the Academy? I would do exactly what you told me."
exchanges.story:
Ysolde turns from the window again.

"A circuit changes the distance, not the answer," she says. "I said not soon."

She breaks another piece from the dark bread and eats it without looking away from her plate.

exchanges.player: "All right. I won't ask again." I return to my breakfast. After the scheduled classes, I go to the dueling grounds and check the notices. If there is a public bout this afternoon, I find a place to watch it through to the result. I have never seen a formal duel before.
exchanges.story:
Ysolde answers your promise with a single nod and returns to her breakfast.

By the time the scheduled classes release for the afternoon, fresh blue ink has gone up on the noticeboard outside the dueling ground: a ranked challenge at fourth bell, public observation permitted. The open octagon is already ringed by students when the bell sounds.

At its center, a narrow-shouldered angel in grey practice clothes faces a beastkin woman with tawny fur at her temples and a padded staff held low. A proctor checks their ward bands, then raises one hand.

"First clean scoring touch. Stop when I call it."

The angel moves first, a white flare skipping from her palm to the packed earth. Her opponent springs clear, closes the distance, and drives the staff toward the angel's ribs. The angel catches the shaft on a brief plane of light. Dust kicks up around their feet as they separate.

The second exchange is shorter. The beastkin fighter feints high, then cuts low. Light flashes at the wrong height. Her staff thumps against the angel's calf before the proctor's hand comes down.

"Touch. Challenge succeeds."

Applause breaks unevenly around the octagon. The defeated student bows, limping only slightly as the ward band cools at her wrist. A clerk pins a revised ranking strip beneath the notice while the small crowd begins to peel away toward the quadrangle.

exchanges.player: I return to Garvey House. Over the following two days I attend my classes, read, and explore the public grounds. At the end of those two days, after classes, I go to the covered court to see whether the practice group has its access back.
exchanges.story:
The next two days pass through lecture bells, library lamps, and the public paths of the Academy. The quadrangle changes character with the hour: crowded between classes, nearly bare at dusk except for the chapel steps and the slow traffic toward the bridges. Garvey House remains busy around meals, then falls into separate rooms and study tables.

After the second day's classes, the covered court door stands open.

A new notice is pinned beside it.

*PROVISIONAL SUPERVISED ACCESS: three evening sessions. Named Academy supervisor required. Equipment inspection before use. Independent practice remains suspended pending review.*

The notice gives no account of the injury.

Inside, the court's high roof holds the late light in long grey strips. Eight students stand spaced across the marked floor with padded staves and practice blades. An Academy instructor in a plain dark coat watches from the center line, correcting grips one at a time.

Rashid is among the group. He lowers his staff when the instructor calls for a reset, then steps back to give a smaller student room to try the sequence again. His folio rests against the wall beside a stack of unused ward bands.

exchanges.player: I watch quietly until the session ends, then approach Rashid. "You got the supervised sessions. I'm glad it worked out."
exchanges.story:
The instructor ends the session at the next bell. Practice weapons go back into the rack one by one; the ward bands are counted before anyone is allowed to leave. Students drift out in small groups, talking over bruised knuckles and missed steps.

Rashid unfastens the wrap at one wrist and reaches for his folio when you approach. At your words, he glances toward the notice by the door.

"For three evenings," he says. "It's less than we had, but people can practice while they decide what to do with the report."

He closes the folio over the remaining copies of the request. "Thessaly caught the problem in the first wording. I might have handed them a petition they could approve without opening the court at all."

The instructor calls for Rashid from the equipment rack. He tucks the folio under his arm and heads across the marked floor.

exchanges.player: I leave Rashid to the instructor and return to Garvey House for dinner. After eating, I go into the common room with a cup of tea. I would like some company tonight, so I look to see what people are doing.
exchanges.story:
Dinner disperses without lingering speeches. By the time you bring tea into the common room, the fire has been built up against the evening chill and only a few lamps are lit.

Thessaly occupies one end of the long table with Rashid's revised request open beside her notebook. She has copied a line from the new notice onto a separate sheet and is comparing the two in silence.

Near the hearth, Seraphel sits in a leather chair with a book open across her lap. The gold at her skin softens in the firelight. She looks up as you enter, then returns to the page without speaking.

Thessaly notices you after a moment. "Rashid left this for me to read before he gives it to anyone else," she says, touching the petition. "The new version names what the Academy must provide. It is better."

She moves her notebook and a spare chair out from the table with one hand. "There is room here."

exchanges.player: I sit in the offered chair. "Is this a further request after the three sessions were approved?" I ask Thessaly.
exchanges.story:
Thessaly sets the petition beside the copied notice and aligns their lower edges.

"No. This is the request that already exists." She points first to the petition's line about a designated supervisor, then to the notice's three-session limit. "The Academy has given it a temporary answer. It has not said what happens when the review ends."

She looks back down at the papers. "If Rashid asks for regular access after that, it will be a further request. It should not pretend otherwise."

From the hearth, Seraphel turns a page in her book. The paper makes a soft, dry sound over the fire.

exchanges.player: "I understand." I leave the papers with Thessaly and turn toward Seraphel. "What are you reading?"
exchanges.story:
Seraphel looks up fully this time and marks her place with one finger. The book's blue cover has been rubbed pale at the corners.

"An old travel journal, western roads.
Its writer dislikes inns—and crows."

She turns the cover outward for you to see the faded gilt title, then lets the book rest open across her lap.

exchanges.player: "What made you choose it?" I settle into the chair to hear her answer.
exchanges.story:
Seraphel rests her thumb against the book's spine.

"She gets lost, complains of rain,
Then finds the same inn twice again.
No grander purpose waits inside.
I wanted that tonight."

The fire gives a low pop behind her chair.

Linden.kind: fresh opening plus 15 adaptive player turns

exchanges.player:
My character: Rowan Garvey. A twenty-three-year-old human man with brown skin, unruly dark hair, and ink-stained fingers, wearing a carefully mended charcoal coat and the inherited Garvey signet. Newly arrived and unsure of Conclave customs. He grew up unaware of his heritage, lost his parents young, and does not know whether he has any magic.

Begin the story shortly before the welcome dinner, in my room at Garvey House. I play Rowan Garvey.
exchanges.story:
Two clear chimes rise from the dining hall, softened by the old wood of Garvey House. Your second-floor room is spare but finished: a made bed beneath a dark green coverlet, clothes sent ahead in a narrow wardrobe, and a desk placed to catch the garden light. Beyond the window, pale paths thread between flowering hedges toward the glow of the bridges over the storm.

The Academy primer lies open beside a small brass lamp. Its thin pages name the seven Council peoples, the welcome dinner, and Article Nineteen in the same clipped type. The inherited signet on your hand bears the Garvey device sharply enough to press a mark into the desk if you lean on it. Across the room, a framed letter in an older hand addresses a great-nephew who never arrived.

Below, chairs scrape over the dining hall floor. A voice says something too low to catch; another answers with a brief laugh. Candlelight reaches the landing through the open stairwell, carrying the smell of roast onions, pepper, and warm bread. A place has been set at the long table for the first human Conclave student in generations.

exchanges.player: I go down to the dining hall. "Good evening. I'm Rowan. I worked in a print shop before the lawyers found me; I'm hoping there is a press here I could use." I look for my place at the table.
exchanges.story:
The dining hall is already bright with candles and warmed plates. Your arrival cuts through a low conversation near the middle of the long table. An ivory place card on the garden side reads ROWAN GARVEY in the Academy's severe hand; the chair beside it stands between Rashid vel Amara and Thessaly Morrow.

Rashid's amber eyes lift from a folded sheet near his plate. Fine dark fur covers the hand he uses to tap the paper flat. “Commerce has a press in the lower annex. You can use it if you book a time. The student journal takes most evening slots, but the board changes after supper.”

Thessaly, small and straight-backed beside the empty place, turns her black eyes toward him. “It says it changes. It often does not.”

“I checked it today,” Rashid says. “There was room tomorrow.”

Across the table, a tall woman with swept-back black-red horns sets down her water glass and resumes eating. Near her, a pale-haired woman studies the flame of a candle without looking up. The folded sheet by Rashid's plate bears several names beneath a heading about the covered court.

A server in Academy livery pauses beside the empty chair with a covered soup bowl.

exchanges.player: "Thank you. I will check it after supper." I take my seat and thank the server, then eat and listen as the conversation continues.
exchanges.story:
Rashid gives a short nod and moves the folded sheet clear of the server's bowl. The soup is sharp with pepper and root vegetables. Around the table, spoons begin to move; wax gathers in small pale pools below the candles.

“You still have the covered court tomorrow,” Rashid says to the horned woman across from him.

Ashara tears a piece of bread. “I have an existing booking.”

“I need your name on the request for supervised access.”

“You need the instructor's report first. You have statements from the students who were there. That isn't the same thing.”

At the far end of the table, Aldric sets down his spoon. “A student was injured. A short closure while the dean reviews it is reasonable.”

Rashid turns toward him. “Do you know whether the equipment failed, whether the instructor ignored it, or whether someone made a mistake?”

“No.”

“Neither do I. But closing it to everyone means the students without private tutors lose their practice time first.”

Ashara takes the sheet from beside Rashid's plate and reads the heading. “Bring me the report when you have it. I will not give up tomorrow's booking.”

“I didn't ask you to.”

She folds the sheet once along its existing crease and sets it beside her glass.

exchanges.player: I finish supper without offering an opinion on the court. Then I go to the Commerce lower annex and check the booking board. I want twelve copies of a short story, two printed pages, and look for the first afternoon slot outside my classes that leaves time for setting type and proofing.
exchanges.story:
Commerce is quieter after supper. The lower annex lies beneath an arcade of low stone arches, its windows lit from within by green-shaded lamps. Through the wire-mesh glass of the print room, a hand press sits under a dust cover beside ranks of wooden type cases.

The booking board occupies the wall outside. A weekly Academy timetable has been pinned beside it, with the first-year Conclave seminars marked in blue. Tomorrow's common session ends at the second afternoon bell. Beneath the press ledger, the first unclaimed pairing begins an hour later: Composing Table Two from the third bell until the fourth, then Hand Press One from the fourth until the sixth. A penciled note in the margin gives new users the composing hour for setting and a proof before the press is inked.

The later afternoon entries are taken by the student journal and a Commerce society circular. This earlier pair is blank. A stub of graphite is tied to the board beneath the empty lines, and the small print at the bottom says bookings must be confirmed with the annex steward before noon.

exchanges.player: I book Composing Table Two from third to fourth bell and Hand Press One from fourth to sixth: twelve copies of a two-page short story, twenty sheets including proofs. Then I return to my room and lay out the finished manuscript I brought with me. I go to bed and sleep until morning; I intend to see the steward before noon to confirm the afternoon booking.
exchanges.story:
The graphite leaves your name, the two afternoon times, and the requested paper allowance in the open spaces on the ledger. The entries above and below are written in different inks and hands; the blank pair now has a clear claim beside it.

Garvey House has quieted by the time you return. In your room, the manuscript comes out in a finished stack. You lay its pages across the desk beneath the brass lamp, with enough room between them to see the margins and corrections already made. The framed letter remains on the wall beyond the desk, its ink faded at the edges of the page.

By morning, the lamp has burned out. The manuscript is still spread beneath the window, and the slip of booking details rests beside it. From the floor below comes the clink of breakfast dishes and the murmur of a servant setting the dining room for the day.

exchanges.player:
I wash, dress, eat breakfast, and take my manuscript to the annex steward before morning instruction. "I'm Rowan Garvey. I booked Composing Table Two at third bell and Hand Press One from fourth to sixth, for twelve copies and twenty sheets including proofs. I've worked in a print shop. Could you confirm the booking?" I offer the manuscript. Its complete text is below; it is fiction, not an account of my own life.

The Umbrella

At closing time Mrs Venn left her umbrella in the print shop. Tobin noticed it while sweeping and ran after her, still wearing his apron.

At the corner a man with a flower in his coat seized his elbow. "They've been waiting for you."

"I've only come to return this."

"Of course you have. This way."

He led Tobin through a kitchen, where someone gave him a bowl of sugared almonds and told him to stand still. Through the next door he could see a bride sitting alone beneath a garland. She had taken off one shoe.

"You aren't the musician," she said.

"No. Is Mrs Venn here?"

"Everyone's here except the musician and the groom."

Tobin offered her the almonds. She took three.

For a while they listened to the guests arguing about where the missing men ought to have been looked for. Someone proposed the north road. Someone else said he had already tried it, though only the nearest tavern.

"I could go," Tobin said.

"Finish those first. Mother counted the bowls."

He remained by the door. The bride put her shoe back on and began removing pins from her hair, setting each one carefully beside her plate.

Mrs Venn finally appeared with the missing musician, who had gone to the wrong wedding and stayed for supper. Tobin held out the umbrella. She took it from him, examined the handle, and frowned.

"This belongs to my sister."

"You brought it to the shop."

"Yes. I was meant to return it yesterday."

The bride stood up. "I'll take it to her."

Mrs Venn opened her mouth, looked at the pins beside the plate, and shut it again. She gave her daughter the umbrella.

"It's not raining," Tobin said.

"It might."

The bride walked out through the kitchen. Tobin moved to follow, but Mrs Venn caught the empty almond bowl before it fell.

"Have you eaten?"

He shook his head.

"Then sit down. We're not sending all this back."

By the time the groom arrived, Tobin had been given his chair. Nobody asked him to move.
exchanges.story:
Breakfast is nearly cleared when you leave Garvey House with the manuscript. The lower annex smells of damp stone and machine oil in the morning. Inside the steward's office, a woman in rolled ink-stained sleeves sits behind a high counter with the booking ledger open before her.

She takes the pages and checks the title, the length, and the margins without hurrying. Her thumb holds the second leaf flat while she compares it with the entry in the ledger.

“Good. Two pages, twelve copies, twenty sheets. That gives you room for proofs.” She writes CONFIRMED in red beside both of the afternoon entries. “Composing Table Two at third bell. Hand Press One from fourth until sixth. Bring the first proof here before you ink the full run.”

She returns the manuscript and tears a narrow receipt from the ledger's duplicate page. The same times and paper allowance are stamped across it in blue, with the annex seal pressed into the lower corner.

exchanges.player: "Thank you." I attend morning instruction, then return to Composing Table Two at third bell. I set my two pages and pull a proof, check it against the manuscript, and take it to the steward as requested. If she approves it, I print the twelve copies, clean up, and collect them once the ink is dry enough to carry.
exchanges.story:
Morning instruction gives way to the third bell. At Composing Table Two, the manuscript lies propped beside the composing stick while the type cases fill the workbench around it. By the time the first proof comes off the small proofing press, the black letters stand in two close pages on the damp sheet.

The steward reads the proof against the manuscript at her counter, following the lines with a metal rule. She checks the outer margins, then turns the sheet beneath the lamp.

“Even impression. The type is locked cleanly. Run your twelve.”

Hand Press One takes the rest of the afternoon in the rhythm of ink, paper, and the long pull of the bar. The first sheets hang across the drying rack; the later ones follow in a dark, orderly row. Before the sixth bell finishes, the cases are back in order and the press bed is clean.

The steward tests the final sheet with the back of one finger, then gathers the twelve copies into a brown-paper wrap. She folds the top over twice, ties it with blue string, and sets the bundle on the counter beside your receipt.

exchanges.player: I take the copies back to Garvey House, leave all but one in my room, and go to the library. I look for someone not already in a conversation. "I've just printed a short comedy. Would you like a copy?" I offer it without pressing it into anyone's hands.
exchanges.story:
At Garvey House, the brown-paper wrap becomes a small stack on your desk, with one unwrapped copy kept aside. The library is lit for the evening when you reach it. Lamp-oil hangs lightly in the air beneath the iron stair, and most of the lower tables are occupied by students bent over their own work.

On the upper gallery, Caelindra Vaeyn has a table to herself near the railing. A thick volume lies open before her, held flat by a silver paperknife. She is copying something from it into a narrow notebook when your offer reaches her.

Her violet eyes settle on the printed pages, then on you. “Two pages,” she says. “That is merciful.”

She sets the paperknife across the open volume and moves a clear space beside it. “Leave it there.”

exchanges.player: I set the copy in the space she cleared. "I'm pleased with how it came out. I'd like to hear what you think when you have time." I leave her to her work, then go down for dinner. I greet the others, sit, and listen while I eat.
exchanges.story:
Caelindra looks down at the copy after you place it beside her book. “When I have read it, I will tell you.” She draws the paperknife back into place and resumes her notes.

The dining hall is louder than the library, with lamps turned high against the dark windows. By the time the first course is served, Rashid arrives carrying two fresh sheets of paper instead of the folded request from the night before. He sets one beside Ashara's plate.

“The dean's office says the review will take three more days,” he says. “I changed the request.”

Thessaly reads the first few lines over the edge of her water glass. “It no longer asks for the court to reopen tomorrow.”

“It asks for supervised access as soon as it does reopen,” Rashid says. “And for the instructor's report to be available to the students who were there.”

Ashara scans the page. “This is narrower.”

“It is.”

She reaches for her pen, pauses over the line beneath the request, and reads the page again while the servers begin to clear the first bowls.

exchanges.player: "That leaves your group without practice for three more days. What made you change the request?" I ask Rashid.
exchanges.story:
Rashid looks from the request to you. “Because the first version asked people to endorse a cause none of us knows.”

He taps the page with one claw-tip. “I can say the closure costs students their practice time. I can't say whether the instructor was negligent or the equipment failed. If I make that claim and the report says otherwise, the dean gets to ignore everything else.”

“The students still lose three days,” Ashara says.

“Yes. But this gives us a request people can sign without pretending they saw the accident.”

Ashara uncaps her pen. “I will sign this one. Not the earlier version.”

She writes her name on the first line and pushes the paper back across the table. Rashid takes it before the ink has fully dried.

exchanges.player: "Could the group practise in the Garvey House gardens for those three days? I would be willing to make space, if we can agree a safe arrangement with the people who use them."
exchanges.story:
Ashara sets her pen down. “Not for ranked practice. The paths are too close, and I won't have anyone throwing a weapon through a hedge because they wanted to prove a point.”

“No weapons,” Rashid says. “Footwork, balance, conditioning. We could keep it to the west lawn and stop before the gardeners need it.”

Thessaly looks toward the dark garden doors. “The west lawn is used after supper. Less often in the late afternoon.”

“Then we ask the people who use it,” Rashid says. “And the gardener. Nobody gets told their walk has become our drill yard.”

Aldric folds his napkin beside his plate. “If it is supervised, with no live magic or sparring, it is a more reasonable request than reopening a closed court.”

Ashara gives the revised petition another look. “It also needs a named person responsible for ending a session if it stops being safe.”

“I can take that,” Rashid says.

He pulls a clean sheet from his folder and writes LIMITED GARDEN PRACTICE across the top. Beneath it, he begins a list of conditions and names to ask before the next afternoon.

exchanges.player: "That sounds reasonable to me." I finish dinner and leave the organizing with Rashid. I spend the rest of the evening reading, then sleep until morning. At breakfast, if Caelindra is there, I ask, "Did you have a chance to read the story?"
exchanges.story:
Rashid keeps the new sheet and the signed petition at his place when dinner ends. The rest of the evening passes in the quiet of your room, with the house settling around you and the garden lamps beyond the window dimming one by one.

At breakfast, Caelindra is already at the long table. Your printed copy lies beside her plate, folded once along its center. She looks up when you ask about it.

“I did.” She rests one fingertip on the paper. “The bowl is the better choice. The umbrella gets Tobin into the room; the bowl tells him he may stay. You stop before explaining it, which is why it works.”

She refolds the copy along its existing crease and sets it beside her cup.

exchanges.player: "Thank you. I'm glad that came across." I attend the day's classes. In the late afternoon I go to the gardens to see whether the temporary practice has been arranged, and stay to watch if it takes place.
exchanges.story:
Late afternoon finds the west lawn marked off with a thin white cord set well back from the paths and flowerbeds. A card tied to the nearest post gives the terms in a gardener's neat hand: SUPERVISED CONDITIONING ONLY. NO WEAPONS. NO LIVE MAGIC. PATHS REMAIN OPEN.

Rashid stands at the center of the grass with six students spaced around him. They move through a sequence of turns and low steps, shoes pressing the lawn flat and then springing free. His sleeves are rolled to his elbows despite the cooling air.

“Again,” he calls. “Slow enough that you know where your weight is.”

A student on the outer edge clips the cord with a heel. Rashid raises one hand, and the group stops before anyone carries the motion farther.

“Reset inside the line. If you need more ground, ask for it. Don't take it.”

They shift inward, leaving the path clear as two Commerce students pass through the gardens with their books under their arms. Rashid waits until they have gone by, then lowers his hand and begins the count for the next sequence.

exchanges.player: I leave the practice with Rashid. Over the next two days I attend classes and work on another story in my room. At dinner at the end of those two days, I ask Rashid, "Did the review finish when they said it would?"
exchanges.story:
The next two days settle into classes, meals, and the growing stack of pages on your desk. By the third evening, Rashid has an Academy envelope tucked beneath his plate.

At your question, he draws out a copied report and smooths it flat against the tablecloth.

“It finished this afternoon. The retaining line on the north practice rig was overdue for replacement. It snapped during a landing drill.”

Ashara reads over the nearest edge of the page. “Was the instructor at fault?”

“The report says he stopped the session properly once it failed. Maintenance had flagged the line weeks ago and never replaced it.” Rashid's finger rests on a paragraph near the bottom. “The court stays closed until a new rig arrives. They estimate five more days.”

He turns the page over. “The dean approved the garden arrangement through then, with the same conditions. The students who attended received this copy.”

The report remains open between the serving dishes, its Academy seal broken along the fold.

exchanges.player: I turn to Aldric. "Does the report change how you see the closure?"
exchanges.story:
Aldric reads the paragraph Rashid indicated before answering.

“It changes how I see the Academy's conduct.” He folds his hands beside the report. “Closing an unsafe court was right. Failing to replace the line after it was flagged was not, and the students should have been told why the court was closed.”

Rashid watches him across the table.

“I was too quick to call the restriction reasonable without knowing what it rested on,” Aldric says. “I will ask the dean why maintenance ignored the report, and why the affected students received it only after the review.”

“Ask in writing,” Rashid says. “Then he has to answer in writing.”

Aldric nods once. “I will.”

exchanges.player: "Then I will leave that with you." I keep attending my classes and working on my second story over the following five days. On the afternoon the repairs were estimated to finish, I go to the covered court to see whether practice can resume there.
exchanges.story:
Over the following days, classes keep their hours and the pages of your second story gather across the desk. The garden practice continues under its posted limits until the afternoon named in the repair notice.

The covered court doors stand open when you reach them. A fresh retaining line runs above the north rig, pale against the darker beams. Near the entrance, an Academy notice bears a new inspector's seal: COURT REOPENED FOR SUPERVISED USE. A second sheet beneath it records the replacement date and the maintenance order number.

Rashid is already inside with the practice group. He checks the line's attachment once, then moves them into the open floor beneath it. The students leave their garden boundary cord coiled by the wall, along with the small sign that had kept the paths clear.

“Pairs,” Rashid says. “Start with the landing sequence. Take the full space this time.”

The first two students step out across the packed court floor as the others spread back to give them room.

Flint.kind: three responses to a constructed starting state

exchanges.player: "I am not looking for a verdict on whether he is a good person. Does the situation hold your interest so far?" I let Caelindra read the three pages. Privately, I wonder whether I have made the keeper too obviously resemble Rashid; I do not say that aloud.
exchanges.story:
Caelindra reads in silence, the library's lamps making a pale edge along her silver hair. She does not turn the pages quickly. On the last, her fingertip rests beside the point where the keeper leaves the light unattended.

"It holds my interest," she says at last. "Because he has not chosen between virtue and vice. He has chosen one duty over another, and neither has agreed to become less necessary for him."

She sets the sheets squarely atop the closed book. "The replacement is where it may become ordinary. If that person simply fails because the plot requires it, then the dark is only punishment. If they have a reason—one the keeper could have learned, or could not—then you have more than a lesson."

Her gaze moves to the tall windows, where the garden paths lie in separate patches of sun. "Don't tell me yet what happens to the ships. At this point, the shore is more interesting. Who sees the lamp go out first? Who decides not to wake anyone? Those people have begun making choices too."

She offers the pages back across the table. "Write until midnight before you decide what the dark cost."

exchanges.player: "Thank you. I will think about the replacement." I take the manuscript back and leave her to her book. At lunch I find Rashid. "Are we still set for this afternoon?" I have not told anyone besides Sela about the changed time or location.
exchanges.story:
Rashid has taken a place near the end of the dining table, with his lunch set aside beside a notebook and two closely written sheets. He looks up from crossing out a line.

"Still set. Sixth bell at the press, as you said." He turns the notebook so the pages do not catch the spill of soup from a passing server. "I cut the claim that the injury came from poor supervision. We don't know that, and it gives Aldric an easy objection. The request asks for two supervised evening sessions next week while they finish the report."

He lays one loose sheet over the other. "Five people have agreed to sign. Two more said they'd read it after practice. I can bring the clean copy at sixth."

Rashid reaches for his cup, then adds, "If you need anything changed, tell me before fifth. I'll be on the court after that."

exchanges.player: "The press has a cracked platen. Sela moved my own work to fourth bell in the west workshop. I can read your revised request now, but I will not print it; my booking is for the story. You will need to arrange the request separately." I hold out my hand for the sheet.
exchanges.story:
Rashid looks from the offered hand to his notebook. He takes the cleaner of the two sheets and puts it into your hand.

"Read it."

He closes the notebook. "I had the sixth-bell arrangement because that's what you gave me. I needed to know the press had failed before I asked people to set aside the evening."

His thumb settles along the notebook's cover. "Fourth is your booking. I won't take it. I'll ask Sela for the next opening after lunch. If she has none today, I can still collect the signatures and circulate the request when it is ready."

He picks up his cup. "Mark any place I've made a claim we cannot stand behind."

established_conversation.content: At dinner I tell Rashid, with Ashara sitting across from us, "I will be at the press tomorrow at sixth bell. You can find me there then."
Rashid puts a small mark beside the appointment in his notebook. "Sixth bell. I can bring the revised request then." Ashara continues eating; neither of them asks about the printing.
Later I go alone to speak to the press steward.

The pressroom is empty except for the steward, Sela. She shows you a crack in the platen. "I cannot run this safely tomorrow. We will have to use the hand press in the west workshop. It is free at fourth bell, if that suits you." The door is shut; the workshop passage outside is quiet.

"Fourth bell in the west workshop is fine. Please leave the change to me; I will tell Rashid myself." I return to my room and keep the change to myself. The next morning I bring three manuscript pages to the library to show Caelindra. My unfinished story concerns a lighthouse keeper who leaves his post to obtain medicine for a sick neighbor. His replacement fails to arrive, and the lighthouse remains dark until midnight. I have not written what happens to any ships or how the story ends.

Caelindra sits at the library window with a book propped against the inkwell. She lays it face-down when you set the pages on the table. "I have a quarter of an hour." She turns the first page. Rashid is elsewhere at morning practice, and nobody else is within earshot.
